headline: NRL expansion into Papua New Guinea has both strong economic and soft-diplomacy rationale given the sport's cultural dominance there
reasoning: Tim Harcourt notes that rugby league is effectively a religion in Papua New Guinea, removing any need for audience conversion, which makes the commercial case straightforward. Beyond economics, he highlights a geopolitical dimension: the PNG franchise serves as soft diplomacy in the Pacific, analogous to rugby union funding in Fiji, and is relevant in the context of Pacific competition with China.

headline: AFL and NRL expansion economics are broadly sound but over-expansion into existing markets risks cannibalization
reasoning: Tim Harcourt argues that franchise expansion generally drives large increases in participation — citing a 40% jump in junior participation following the Tassie Devils' introduction — which in turn grows the talent pool. However, he cautions that expanding too fast or placing too many teams in a single city can dilute the product and cannibalize existing markets, pointing to the A-League's struggles after adding multiple teams in Melbourne and Sydney as a cautionary example.
quote: When you have a new franchise, you get huge increases in participation. For instance, uh, Tassie Devils in the AFL, you know, 40% increase in participation at junior rates, boys and girls. So you tend to find you end up with the growth in talent to to go into the league. So um, they're pretty confident expansions okay. Now you can't expand too fast. I think the A League in soccer had the issue where they put three teams in Melbourne and Sydney, MacArthur and Western United and ran into a bit of a problem. So you do have to concern yourself with how many teams you have in a city if you're going to expand and also, uh, you know, not wanting to crowd or cannibalize to many existing markets.

headline: Private equity investment in Australian sports leagues is unusual but growing, attracting international attention
reasoning: Tim Harcourt notes he has been researching this topic for Deloitte Access Economics and observes that private equity buying into sports leagues is common overseas — in the English Premier League, North American sports, and the IPL — but the majority acquisition of Melbourne Storm by a Swedish private equity firm is unusual for Australia. The deal has attracted coverage in the Financial Times and other financial publications precisely because it is so uncommon in the Australian context.
